prompt: `tcpdump -i eth0`, run by `ana` on `web1`, answered `You don't have permission to perform this capture`. Why?
hint: What does opening the interface let a program read?

choices.text: web1 has no interface called eth0
choices.why: It has; the same command with sudo captured on it.

choices.text: Capturing needs root, or a granted capability
choices.why: Right. web1 has no wireshark group, so it is sudo.

choices.text: A capture filter is compulsory for ordinary users
choices.why: No filter makes an unprivileged capture possible.

choices.text: tcpdump refuses to print to a terminal without -n
choices.why: The first capture with sudo had no -n and worked.

prompt: Without `-n`, `tcpdump` printed port 80 as `http`. Why is `-n` the better habit on a server?
hint: What does turning a number into a name cost?

choices.text: With `-n` tcpdump captures more of the packets
choices.why: What is captured does not change; only how it is printed.

choices.text: Without `-n` the addresses are hidden from view
choices.why: They were printed in full in both runs.

choices.text: `-w` refuses to write a file unless it is given
choices.why: A file stores packets, not printed names; -w works either way.

choices.text: Names cost lookups and hide the real number
choices.why: Right. A reverse lookup per address, and a port named http hides whether it is 80.

prompt: What does `Flags [S.]` say about a packet?
hint: The dot is a flag too.

choices.text: SYN and ACK: the server accepting a connection
choices.why: Right. The second packet of every handshake.

choices.text: SYN alone, with the dot closing the list
choices.why: A lone SYN prints as [S]; the dot is ACK.

choices.text: A SYN that the client had to send a second time
choices.why: A retransmission looks identical to the original in tcpdump.

choices.text: SYN and PUSH: data already in the very first packet
choices.why: Push prints as P; this one has length 0.

prompt: An ACK shows `win 63`, and the SYN of the same connection carried `wscale 10`. What is the real window, in bytes?
hint: The scale is a power of two: 2 to the 10th.

prompt: To stop the laptop reaching `web1`, somebody adds a rule on `web1` dropping `192.168.10.20`. What happens?
hint: Which source address did web1's capture show?

choices.text: The laptop is cut off, and the rest of the office is not
choices.why: web1 never sees 192.168.10.20; the rule matches nothing.

choices.text: Nothing: the laptop arrives as 203.0.113.2
choices.why: Right. hq translates the office's addresses, so the rule would need hq's public one, and that is the whole office.

choices.text: Every connection from hq is dropped
choices.why: That would take a rule on 203.0.113.2, not on the private address.

choices.text: The laptop gets a reset instead of a page
choices.why: A drop sends nothing back, and this one never matches anyway.

prompt: Put the flags of a connection opening and its first request in the order tcpdump prints them.
hint: The client speaks first and last.
trap: The request cannot go before the handshake's last ACK, and the server answers the SYN before anything else.

prompt: What does `-Z ana` do in `sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 -c 40 -Z ana -w web1.pcap tcp port 80`?
hint: Look at who owns the file.

choices.text: Makes the file readable by ana and nobody else
choices.why: The file came out -rw-r--r--, readable by everyone; -Z decides the owner, not the mode.

choices.text: Drops root after opening the interface
choices.why: Right. It becomes ana before writing, so the parsing runs unprivileged and the file is hers.

choices.text: Compresses the file as it is written
choices.why: capinfos found an ordinary pcap file.

choices.text: Captures only ana's own traffic
choices.why: Packets carry addresses, not user names; the filter decides what is kept.

prompt: `capinfos` reported a file size of 4690 bytes and a data size of 4026 bytes for 40 packets. The pcap file header is 24 bytes. How many bytes does the format add in front of each packet?
hint: Take away the file header, then share what is left.

prompt: Why compare the `SHA256` line of `capinfos` on the server and on the analyst's copy?
hint: A hash changes if a single byte does.

choices.text: To decrypt the packets inside
choices.why: A hash decrypts nothing; it identifies bytes.

choices.text: To prove who took the capture
choices.why: Anybody computing it gets the same line; it says nothing about the author.

choices.text: Same line, same bytes
choices.why: Right. Nothing lost, nothing edited on the way.

choices.text: To check the capture filter was right
choices.why: The hash is of the file as written, right filter or wrong.

prompt: `web1.pcap` came out `-rw-r--r--`. On a server other people log into, what does that mean?
hint: r-- for the others.

choices.text: Any account can read the traffic in it
choices.why: Right. chmod 600 after, or umask 077 before.

choices.text: Only root can open it, because root captured it
choices.why: The file belongs to ana, and the last r lets everyone else read it.

choices.text: Nobody but ana can read it
choices.why: That would be -rw-------, the mode tshark used.

choices.text: Other users can add packets to it
choices.why: Only the owner has w.

prompt: Why did `tcpdump -n -r web1.pcap` need no `sudo`?
hint: It opens a file, not an interface.

choices.text: Because the capture used `-n`
choices.why: -n is about names, not permission.

choices.text: Because tcpdump keeps root from the capture
choices.why: Nothing is kept; each run starts as whoever typed it.

choices.text: Reading a file ana owns needs no privilege
choices.why: Right. Only opening an interface does.

choices.text: A pcap file carries its own permission to be read
choices.why: The file system decides, like for any file.

prompt: `tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0` printed eight lines from `web1.pcap`: a SYN and a SYN-ACK each time. How many connections were opened?
hint: Two lines per connection.

prompt: Read with a filter that hid the handshake, a server's answer acknowledged `73`; the full read had shown `74`. A colleague says a byte was lost. What happened?
hint: Relative to what?

choices.text: One byte was lost on the way and retransmitted later
choices.why: The file has no retransmission; the packets are the same ones.

choices.text: The server acknowledged one byte too few by mistake
choices.why: The server sent the same packet both times; only the printing differs.

choices.text: tcpdump counted from the request, not the SYN
choices.why: Right. Without the SYN the base moves by one; -S prints raw numbers and ends the confusion.

choices.text: -A shifts the numbering by one to fit the text
choices.why: -A changes how the payload is printed, not the header's numbers.

prompt: To make `tcpdump` print raw sequence numbers on every packet, add the flag ___ to the command.
hint: Capital letter; the small one is the snap length.

prompt: Reading `short.pcap`, a line ended in `[|http]`. What does it mean?
hint: The file was captured with -s 96.

choices.text: The server answered with an HTTP error
choices.why: This was the request, and nothing in it is an error.

choices.text: The packet was damaged on the wire
choices.why: It arrived whole; the capture kept only its start.

choices.text: The stored copy stops inside the HTTP
choices.why: Right. The snap length cut it after 96 bytes.

choices.text: The output was piped into another program
choices.why: The pipe to head only limits lines; the mark is tcpdump's.

prompt: With `-s 96`, Ethernet, IP and TCP took 14, 20 and 32 bytes. How many bytes of the HTTP request were kept?
hint: 96 minus the headers.

prompt: After `-C 1 -W 3` the ring held `ring.pcap0` of 237648 bytes and two files of about a million. Which holds the newest packets?
hint: Which one was not full?

choices.text: ring.pcap2, the highest number
choices.why: The numbers are the order of creation, and the ring wrapped round.

choices.text: ring.pcap0, the one not full
choices.why: Right. It was being overwritten when the capture stopped.

choices.text: ring.pcap1, in the middle
choices.why: That one holds the oldest packets still kept.

choices.text: All three, with packets mixed across them
choices.why: Each file is written in turn, never two at once.

prompt: A ring of `-C 100 -W 5` runs overnight. The fault happened at 02:00 and you stop the capture at 09:00. When will the 02:00 packets be missing?
hint: How much can the ring hold?

choices.text: Never: a ring keeps the whole night
choices.why: It keeps five files of 100 million bytes, whatever the night was.

choices.text: Only if the capture filter was wrong
choices.why: A right filter still fills files; the ring still wraps.

choices.text: If over about 500 MB came after 02:00
choices.why: Right. Stop it close to the fault, or size the ring to the traffic.

choices.text: If the capture ran longer than five hours
choices.why: The ring counts bytes, not hours.

prompt: Which of these reduce what a capture file exposes about other people? Choose all that apply.
hint: Less in the file, or less time with the file.

choices.text: A short snap length
choices.why: Right: headers without contents.

choices.text: The `-n` flag
choices.why: It changes the printing, and the file keeps the same packets.

choices.text: A capture filter for one host and port
choices.why: Right: other people's traffic is never recorded.

choices.text: Deleting the file once the question is answered
choices.why: Right: a file that is gone exposes nothing.

choices.text: Reading it with `-A`
choices.why: That prints the contents, which is the opposite.

prompt: `tshark -z http,tree` counted 8 HTTP packets in `web1.pcap`, which holds 40. What are the other 32?
hint: Four connections, each opened and closed.

choices.text: Packets the kernel dropped
choices.why: tcpdump reported 0 dropped by kernel.

choices.text: HTTP packets cut short by the snap length
choices.why: web1.pcap was captured whole, with the default length.

choices.text: Encrypted HTTPS that tshark cannot count
choices.why: The capture filter was tcp port 80; nothing on 443 was kept.

choices.text: TCP packets that open, acknowledge and close
choices.why: Right. Eight carry HTTP; the rest are TCP doing its own work.

prompt: The analysis is finished and the ticket is closed. What should happen to the capture files?
hint: They are copies of other people's data.

choices.text: Keep them for six months in case the fault returns
choices.why: A new fault gets a new capture; the old one only keeps exposing people.

choices.text: Move them to /tmp, where the system clears them
choices.why: /tmp is readable by others and cleared on nobody's schedule you control.

choices.text: Delete every copy
choices.why: Right. On the server and everywhere else, and say so in the ticket.

choices.text: Compress them so they take less space
choices.why: A compressed capture holds exactly the same data.

prompt: A production web server returns an occasional HTTP 500 and you are asked to capture it. Which command is proportionate?
hint: Bounded in size, one port, not root, to a file.

choices.text: `sudo tcpdump -i any -w all.pcap`
choices.why: Every interface, every protocol, and no end: the opposite of proportionate.

choices.text: `sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 -C 10 -W 4 -Z ana -w web.pcap tcp port 80`
choices.why: Right. One port, a ring of 40 MB, and root dropped before writing.

choices.text: `sudo tcpdump -n -A -i eth0 tcp port 80`, watching the screen
choices.why: It prints every form to a terminal and keeps nothing to analyse.

choices.text: `tcpdump -n -i eth0 -w web.pcap tcp port 80`
choices.why: Without sudo it is refused before it captures anything.
